title: Salt in the water
word: reading the Isha in the original
hookLine: salt dissolved in water, and the Isha's riddle: that moves and moves not
carry: the one reality is far, near, and inside all this
tomorrow: can the order of words teach something all on its own?

cards: Sit on a train at a station, and when the train beside you starts to roll, there's a second where you honestly can't tell which one is moving. Still and moving at once, until you look out the other window.
The Isha builds its next two verses on that second. Tad ejati tan naijati. That moves.
That moves not. And it never names what that is. It just keeps pointing: tad, that, again and again, like something too big for a label.

teach.h: MOVES AND NOT, FAR AND NEAR.
teach.b: Verse four sets it up: anejad ekam manaso javiyo, unmoving, one, swifter than the mind. Verse five: tad ejati tan naijati. That moves, that moves not.
Na, not, and ejati, moves, melt into naijati, one syllable holding a whole no. Then: tad dure, that is far; tad v antike, that is near. That is inside all this, and outside all this.
To hear what that is, borrow a story from another Upanishad, the Chandogya.
A father, Uddalaka, tells his son Shvetaketu to drop a lump of salt in water overnight. In the morning: bring me the salt. The boy can't find it.
Sip from the top, says the father. Salty. The middle?
It's there all along, the father says; you just can't see it.

teach.h: TAT TVAM ASI: YOU ARE THAT.
teach.b: That finest thing is the self of all this, and you are that: tat tvam asi. Here's the teaching.
Brahman, the one reality, is beyond everything, faster than the mind, and also dissolved in every sip of the world, including you.
Hindu schools read it differently: Advaita hears one reality and nothing else; Vishishtadvaita hears the Lord inside all he pervades.

Now hold up the week: dharma kept at home, a despair that starts the path, the Lord in all this, offering before enjoying, action that doesn't bind, the self worth more than the world. And now the salt: that, everywhere.

how: Hindu schools read these verses differently: Advaita teachers hear one reality beyond motion and place, while Vishishtadvaita teachers hear the Lord present in, and beyond, all he pervades.

games.q: what does “reading the isha in the original” mean?
o: the Isha's verses about trains and travel
salt in the water, and that which is far and near
a riddle with no answer at all

games.q: the week, word by word — tap the pairs.
p: you are that: the salt in every sip

s: the Isha contradicts itself by mistake in verse five
the pairs are deliberate: moves and moves not, far and near.
in naijati, the word for not is melted into one syllable
na plus ejati becomes naijati: a whole no in nai.
every Hindu school reads 'that' in these verses in exactly the same way
Advaita hears one reality and nothing else; Vishishtadvaita hears the Lord inside all he pervades.

games.q: a classmate reads 'that moves, that moves not' and says, 'so it's just confused.' what's the reader's answer?
o: the pairs are on purpose: each one stops a picture from settling.
it's a copying error; one of the lines should be deleted.
it means that moved once, long ago, and stopped.
games.why: still and swifter than the mind, far and near, inside and outside: every pair stops a single picture, because Brahman is beyond them and in them, like salt in water.

practice: Keep the body still and listen for one sound that moves: traffic, wind, a fan, someone in the next room. Let it come close and go far while you stay where you are. Still, and the sound moving through: both true at once.
If you pray, end with one quiet Om, the sound many Hindus use to point at that.

wordCard.voice: Reading the Isha in the original, verses four and five: that which moves and moves not, far and near, inside all this, like salt in the water.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: naijati, na plus ejati, moves not, with the not melted in.

carryVoice: Your line: the one reality is far, near, and inside all this. Brahman, salty top to bottom. That's the week; rest well.
